title: Is there a canon beyond chance?
question: Do neuron units pick out a core that random sets of films lack?
result: Yes. No random 32-film set has a single neuron present in 23 or more of its films; Batman has 1,534 (Qwen3-8B). Names were present, so much of this core is name detectors.
method: 50 random 32-film pseudo-franchises against the 32 Batman works.
rivals: None run for this count.
premise: P1: the unit is countable and repeatable. It does not show the unit is a concept.

title: Blind test of the meme labels
question: Can a blind judge match a neuron's label to a new sentence it fires on?
result: 56 of 71 right (79%). A judge that only compares word stems gets 65%. For the 31 showcase memes the gap is not significant (77% against 63%, p = 0.07). Judges were AI; item-level answers were not kept.
method: Two-choice test on held-out sentences.
rivals: Word-stem overlap judge.
premise: P1: labels carry some meaning beyond chance, little beyond words.

title: Ideas or words: the rewording test
question: Does a unit still fire when its top sentence is rewritten with no shared content words?
result: 11 of 31 Qwen units passed a lenient bar (5.0 expected by chance). Only 2 Qwen units and 6 Llama units were specific to their own rewording. Every Qwen character unit but one failed without the name.
method: 31 rewritten sentences, scored against ten everyday sentences and a mismatched-rewording null.
rivals: Mismatched rewording.
premise: P1: a few units track ideas; most track words.

title: One concept unit: revenge
question: Is there a neuron for revenge that works without revenge words?
result: Llama's unit chose the revenge sentence in 10 of 12 new minimal pairs. Qwen's unit, picked the same way, scored 4 of 12: it was a keyword detector. The two units correlate at only 0.39.
method: Unit chosen on 10 practice pairs, scored on 12 new pairs with no revenge words.
rivals: The keyword itself.
premise: P1: possible for some concepts in some models. P2: the two models did not agree.

title: Twins across two companies' models
question: Does each Qwen meme have a matching neuron in Llama?
result: The 33 strongest have twins at median r = 0.82, but equally word-like non-meme units reach 0.86. Across all 14,843 families the median is 0.40 against 0.36 for random units. Without names the same pairs fall to 0.14.
method: Best-correlated Llama unit over 3,700 sentences, with nulls matched on sparsity, layer and word-likeness.
rivals: Word-matched non-meme units.
premise: P2: name and word detectors recur. Concept units recur weakly.

title: Do two models draw the same tree?
question: Do Qwen and Llama agree on which works carry which memes and how works relate?
result: Distance matrices correlate at 0.98, but random units give 0.90 to 0.93 and two word methods agree at 0.92. Presence grids agree at kappa 0.73 against 0.35 to 0.57 for controls.
method: Mantel correlation and Cohen's kappa, with random-unit and TF-IDF floors.
rivals: Random units; TF-IDF against LSA.
premise: P2: agreement is mostly a floor any text representation reaches, with a small excess.

title: A smaller sibling model
question: Does Qwen3-1.7B, from the same family, agree better than a different company's model?
result: No. Median twin r is 0.40, the same as for Llama. The agreement level seems to reflect the text more than shared training. Never run on name-free texts.
method: Same pipeline on Qwen3-1.7B.
rivals: Random active units (0.36).
premise: P2: no extra convergence within a model family.

title: Vision neurons on posters
question: Do image-model neurons find Batman memes in posters and covers?
result: Exploratory. CLIP has 56 neurons present in 6 or more of 29 Batman images against 0.6 by chance. No cheap rival was compared and it is not part of the paper.
method: CLIP RN50x4 and DINOv2 neurons on one image per work.
rivals: None.
premise: P2 across media: untested in any strict sense.
bio: The same gene in another tissue

title: Family trees from meme sets
question: Does a tree built from shared memes put each adaptation next to its source comic?
result: No. The source ranks 5.4 of 12 by tree distance against 5.8 by chance. Word counts put it at 2.9, and random non-meme units beat the selected memes in every draw.
method: Jaccard distance on meme sets, neighbour joining.
rivals: TF-IDF, LSA, random units. All won.
premise: P1: the selected 'memes' were worse than unselected units, so the selection rule is suspect.

title: Heredity: adaptations carry their sources
question: With every name removed, do adaptations carry their documented source comic's optional units more than other comics'?
result: Yes, in both models: 16% and 10% of comics beat the source against 47% by chance (exact p = 0.0026 and 0.00017), in 99.6% of 30,240 analysis variants. Word counts do as well (11%).
method: Pre-registered E2: 9 adaptations, 12 comics, exact permutation test.
rivals: TF-IDF cosine and word presence. They matched the neurons.
premise: Shows heredity is measurable in these texts. Does not show neurons are needed.

title: Do neurons add anything beyond shared words?
question: After word similarity is regressed out, does neuron inheritance still point to the source?
result: Not for Qwen (p = 0.09 to 0.25). Marginally for Llama (p = 0.010 to 0.033), but that falls to 0.057 to 0.065 under the stricter nulls and is uncorrected for six tests. Word counts keep their signal with neurons removed.
method: Pre-registered residual test over 32 by 12 pairs.
rivals: TF-IDF and word presence.
premise: The key test of P1's added value. Failed on the primary model.
bio: Signal left after controlling for population structure

title: The vigilante lineage
question: Do the Scarlet Pimpernel, Zorro, Batman and Iron Man show up as one family?
result: Partly. They share the superhero layer (the secret identity) and not Batman's own trappings. One summary each, names present, Zorro only 9 sentences: inconclusive.
method: Nearest relatives and six orphan-vigilante memes across 13 relatives.
rivals: None.
premise: Illustrative only.

title: Identity: what makes a story Batman?
question: Without names, does the share of Batman's canon a work carries separate Batman from other masked heroes?
result: No: AUC 0.52 and 0.54 against 8 hero films, where a word-based score gets 0.80 and text length alone 0.76. It does separate Batman from ordinary films (0.90 to 0.95).
method: Pre-registered E1, held-out works, name-free texts.
rivals: TF-IDF centroid and text length. Both won.
premise: P1: the canon-share score missed what words caught.

title: The name-free core is the superhero template
question: What is left of Batman's core when names are removed?
result: Seven Qwen units: a secret identity, an origin in loss, a costume, a mission by night. They are present in 91% of the hero films too. The neurons rediscovered the standard definition of a superhero. Descriptive, not a test.
method: Units present in at least 70% of name-free Batman works.
rivals: None.
premise: Suggestive for P1: the surviving units are concept-like.

title: Selection: do popular works' memes spread?
question: Do memes carried by popular early works spread further into later works?
result: No signal: rho = 0.25 (p = 0.35) and 0.00 (p = 0.58). The test had 15 works and would catch a true correlation of 0.3 only 27% of the time. A weak null.
method: Pre-registered E3: pageviews against residualised spread.
rivals: Reverse-time placebo.
premise: Says nothing about P1 or P2. Selection needs a bigger lineage and success measured at release.

title: When memes enter and where they recur
question: Can each meme's first appearance and later spread be placed on a timeline?
result: Yes, descriptively. But 6 of 15 optional memes 'first appear' in 1986 only because the sample has no works from 1967 to 1985.
method: First appearance of each named meme among the 32 works.
rivals: None.
premise: Shows the bookkeeping works. The sample is too thin for any claim.

title: Planted memes: neurons against keywords
question: When a meme is written into a story without its usual words, do neurons detect it better than a keyword analyst or a word classifier?
hypothesis: H1 of the pre-registration: neurons beat both word rivals by at least 0.05 AUC on reworded stories.
falsifier: The gap is credibly below 0.05 AUC against either rival.
data: 816 stories to be written (136 plots in 6 versions), 3 of 34 memes planted in each. Truth is known by construction.
method: Each planted story against its own control version, per meme.
rivals: Evasion-aware keyword lists and TF-IDF logistic regression.
premise: P1. The cleanest planned test of whether neurons see ideas when words change.
cost: L: about 4,400 agent sessions and 3 days as designed; a trimmed version takes 1.5 days
risk: Power is only 0.22 to 0.40 at the smallest effect of interest, and every story, reader and rater is one AI model family.

title: Planted memes: neurons against embeddings
question: Are neurons at least as good as the strongest sentence embeddings at finding a planted meme?
hypothesis: H2: neurons are within 0.05 AUC of Qwen3-Embedding-4B and e5-large.
falsifier: Neurons are credibly worse than any one of the three embedding rivals by more than 0.05.
data: The same 816 planted stories.
method: Non-inferiority test, then superiority.
rivals: Qwen3-Embedding-4B on sentences and on 3-sentence windows; e5-large.
premise: P1. If embeddings win, the case for neurons rests on being nameable and cheap, not on accuracy.
cost: L: shares the planted-story run
risk: Power 0.22 when the two are truly equal.

title: Do Batman's concept units travel to other genres?
question: Do the 11 concept units found on Batman texts respond to their own meme, and only that meme, in unrelated stories?
hypothesis: H3: each unit's detection of its own meme exceeds its detection of other memes by at least 0.05 AUC.
falsifier: Specificity credibly below 0.05: the units fire on any eventful passage.
data: The planted stories, in genres far from Batman.
method: Own-meme AUC minus other-meme AUC, labels permuted across units.
rivals: Label permutation; the same test for word and name units.
premise: P1. Tests whether a unit found in one corpus is a portable concept.
bio: Does a gene do the same job in another species
cost: L: shares the planted-story run
risk: Power 0.14 at the smallest effect of interest.

title: Is one neuron enough?
question: Does a single neuron detect a meme as well as five, and does the neuron basis beat the same model's dense hidden states?
hypothesis: 'Single neurons are memes' is claimed only if five neurons beat one by less than 0.03 AUC.
falsifier: Five neurons, or the pooled hidden state, clearly beat one neuron.
data: The planted stories.
method: One unit against five; neurons against hidden states at four layers.
rivals: The model's own hidden states.
premise: P1. Asks whether the neuron is the right unit or just one readout of a dense representation.
bio: One gene or a polygenic trait
cost: L: shares the planted-story run

title: Are neurons easier to name than topics?
question: Can blind judges match labels to neurons better than to LDA topics or embedding clusters?
hypothesis: Neuron labels beat a word-overlap floor and are at least as nameable as topics and clusters.
falsifier: Topics or clusters are as nameable; neurons do not beat the word floor.
data: Labels written for units, topics and clusters on the planted stories.
method: Blind two-choice label test, 12 tests.
rivals: LDA topics, embedding clusters, word-overlap judge.
premise: P1: nameability is the one advantage claimed for neurons over embeddings.
cost: M: about 1,300 agent sessions; first candidate to cut

title: Natural summaries annotated by hand
question: On real plot summaries labelled exhaustively for memes, which method agrees best with the annotators?
hypothesis: Neurons match annotators at least as well as keywords and embeddings.
falsifier: They trail both.
data: 237 name-masked natural summaries, to be annotated.
method: Two annotators plus an adjudicator; each method scored against them.
rivals: Keywords, embeddings, LLM reading.
premise: P1 on natural text.
cost: M: about 600 agent sessions. Deferred
risk: AI annotators recognise masked works and label from memory. Needs human annotators to mean much.

title: Heredity across languages
question: Do neurons still find the source comic when the adaptation's summary is in Chinese and the comic's is in English?
hypothesis: Neurons recover sources across languages where word overlap cannot.
falsifier: Neurons fall to chance, or trail multilingual embeddings and machine translation plus word counts.
data: The Batman lineage translated into Simplified Chinese; a natural zh.wikipedia arm.
method: The E2 statistic across languages.
rivals: Machine translation plus TF-IDF; multilingual embeddings.
premise: Both. Shared wording cannot carry the signal, so a pass would be the first clear win over words.
bio: The same gene in a different genome
cost: M: about 850 agent sessions. Deferred
risk: Chinese is not a supported Llama 3.1 language; translators may bring back the canonical names.

title: Concept agreement on held-out films
question: Do 27 Qwen concept units have Llama partners that agree on 1,000 unseen random films better than word-matched control units?
hypothesis: Concept units agree across models more than 81 lexically matched null units.
falsifier: No advantage over the word-matched nulls on held-out text.
data: 1,000 random film summaries already collected (preregistration/sources/t3_random_films.jsonl.gz).
method: Twins fixed on development text, scored on held-out films.
rivals: Lexically matched non-meme units.
premise: P2. The first out-of-sample test of cross-model agreement. Data is already in hand.
cost: S: extraction on 1,000 summaries. Deferred

title: The vocabulary drift ladder
question: As more of an adaptation's content words are replaced, how long does each method still find its source?
hypothesis: H4: neurons keep finding the source at 50 to 100% replacement where TF-IDF and LSA lose it.
falsifier: Neurons degrade as fast as word counts.
data: Batman and Shakespeare-film summaries rewritten at 25, 50, 75 and 100% replacement, with a style-only control.
method: Source recovery at each level.
rivals: TF-IDF, LSA. Embeddings and an LLM reader should be added.
premise: P1. A lineage where wording changes and ideas stay is exactly what the paper says is needed.
cost: M: about 850 agent sessions. Deferred
risk: Power 0.15 at the smallest effect of interest; the rewriter may leak source words.

title: Shakespeare: a fresh lineage
question: Do loose film adaptations of Shakespeare carry their play's memes when names, settings and wording all differ?
hypothesis: H5: neurons rank the true play above other plays for renamed adaptations.
falsifier: No better than chance, or no better than words.
data: 40 plays and 54 films of 13 plays with documented sources (preregistration/works_shakespeare.json).
method: E2-style source recovery.
rivals: TF-IDF, LSA.
premise: P1 on a second lineage.
cost: M. Deferred
risk: Ground truth is weaker than it looks: 27 of 83 loose films rested on a Wikipedia category; Romeo and Juliet dominates. Power 0.17.

title: Batman-likeness across 2,544 works
question: Scored on Batman's own units, do documented Batman relatives rank above a large pool of other works?
hypothesis: Documented relatives (Zorro, the Pimpernel, Iron Man and others) rank above the pool.
falsifier: They do not, or TF-IDF, LSA and embeddings rank them as well.
data: 2,544 name-masked works, 62,879 sentences, with 36 documented relatives (preregistration/culture_pool.json).
method: Rank relatives against the pool.
rivals: TF-IDF, LSA, embeddings, an LLM 'likeness' judge.
premise: Uses both. Finds the other billionaire vigilante orphans in the culture.
cost: M. Deferred
risk: Franchises are not independent works; earlier drafts had Batman stories among the negatives.

title: Mutation and selection against a neutral model
question: Are units that first appear in landmark works carried forward more than random copying predicts?
hypothesis: Units new in The Dark Knight Returns, Year One and The Killing Joke spread more than a margin-preserving null allows.
falsifier: Spread is no greater than the neutral model's.
data: 71 Batman works (32 development, 39 test).
method: New units per work, tested against a neutral random-copying model.
rivals: The same test on words.
premise: Uses both. The first population-level test.
cost: M. Deferred
risk: Circular: the added works include direct adaptations of the predicted innovators, and 42 of 43 new works are from 1995 on.

title: Cost against accuracy, head to head
question: Is any rival method both at least as accurate as neurons and no more expensive per story?
hypothesis: H6: no rival dominates.
falsifier: Any rival is at least as accurate and no dearer.
data: The planted stories; timings already measured.
method: Cost per story at 34 memes against accuracy, 17 methods.
rivals: Keywords, embeddings, topics, LLM judges, NLI.
premise: Practical value. One neuron pass costs about as much as one uncached LLM yes-or-no question.
cost: L: shares the planted-story run

title: Catching coded language
question: When a group renames an idea with an invented code word, do methods that read context still find it?
hypothesis: Neurons, hidden states and an LLM judge beat sentence embeddings and keyword lists on code-word versions.
falsifier: Context-free methods do as well.
data: Code-word versions of the planted stories.
method: Six tests on Qwen; the headline is stated only if all six pass.
rivals: Evasion-aware keywords, sentence embeddings.
premise: P1, and a use: moderation when vocabulary is changed to evade filters.
bio: Detecting a gene under a different name
cost: L: shares the planted-story run
risk: Invented code words are not real evasive language. No real-world corpus is in the plan.

title: Held-out twin census with word-matched nulls
question: What share of Qwen3-8B units have a Llama-3.1-8B twin on unseen text once words, sentence length and position in the plot are accounted for?
hypothesis: At least 2% of sampled Qwen units have a twin (the best-correlated Llama unit, chosen on other films) whose held-out correlation beats a rotation baseline by 0.5. At least half of those keep a partial correlation of 0.3 after the word, length and position predictors are removed, mostly at 40 to 60% depth.
falsifier: Fewer than 0.5% of units pass, or fewer than one passer in ten keeps partial correlation 0.3, on original and name-masked text alike. Either refutes neuron-level P2 beyond shared vocabulary. Between 0.5% and 2% is inconclusive. A layer-stratified sample of 20,000 units gives a standard error near 0.1 percentage points.
data: The 1,000 random film plots already committed (`preregistration/sources/t3_random_films.jsonl.gz`; 22,225 sentences after the 40-sentence cap; Wikipedia text, CC BY-SA 4.0). A name-masked copy is not committed: make it with an open entity tagger and hand-check 200 sentences for leaks. Split by film: 500 to choose twins, 500 to score. No Batman text.
method: Unit: each sign of each MLP channel (a hidden neuron), strongest value per sentence. For each sampled Qwen unit, pick the best-correlated Llama unit on one half, keeping mutual picks; score on the other half. Statistics: correlation above a random rotation of Llama's layer (Gurnee's baseline); partial correlation given word, length and position predictors. Null: sentences misaligned between models.
rivals: Each Qwen unit is also predicted from its best single word, a 10-word lasso (a regression that keeps few words), a ridge fit on all words and word pairs, a sentence-embedding ridge, sentence length and position, and Llama's mean-pooled residual stream; an LLM reader only for labelled units. The all-word ridge is most dangerous: if it wins, twins are vocabulary.
premise: P2. A pass gives a counted core of shared units to seed a common catalogue. A fail means 'the same neurons' gives way to 'the same directions', and twin strength stops being a mark of a real meme, because it selects word detectors.
bio: Orthologue census by reciprocal best hits.
cost: S. Four extraction passes of under ten minutes each (two models, two text versions), a few hours of correlation on the laptop, no API spend. Stored whole, the activations take about 80 GB, so process them layer by layer.
payoff: The first cross-family neuron census on 8B models, with held-out numbers to replace the in-sample 0.82 and 0.40 (`nulls.json`, `phylo.json.gz`), and a list of beyond-word shared units that every later cross-model design reuses. The study's 125 labelled units and 27 concept units are scored as fixed subgroups.
risk: The pass share moves with the 0.5 threshold, which Gurnee et al. say has no principled value, so the whole curve is reported. A word control fitted on 11,000 sentences can miss rare synonyms and inflate the beyond-word share; known single-word detectors (best-word correlation 0.9 or more) should fail the test, and their pass rate measures that leak.
review: Added sentence length and plot position to the controls (shared position detectors would otherwise pass as beyond-word twins), an all-word control, and a leak check on known word detectors. The name-masked copy does not exist yet. Remaining weakness: rare synonyms can slip past any word control.
sources: Gurnee et al. 2024; Gröger, Wen and Brbić 2026; study/results/robustness/nulls.json; preregistration T5 (S20), which this supersedes

title: Same story, another language, another model
question: When a story is retold in another language and no words are shared, do unit readings still match, within one model and between Qwen and Llama?
hypothesis: On name-replaced summaries, units find the same story across languages (German original against an English summary) at half or more of the rate they reach when both are read in English; the measure is top-1, the right story ranked first among all test stories. Qwen reading German against Llama reading English keeps half or more of the within-model rate.
falsifier: The cross-language rate is under a quarter of the same-language rate, or no better than random units matched on firing rate, or the cross-model rate is under a quarter of the within-model rate. At least 1,000 qualifying test stories (count them before registering) make a 5-point paired gap about 3 standard errors.
data: Tell Me Again (Hatzel and Biemann 2024): 96,831 Wikipedia plot summaries of 29,505 stories in English, German, French, Italian and Spanish, with supplied machine translations into English, name-replaced versions and an 80/10/10 split (test: 2,951 stories). A 1.7 GB download; text CC BY-SA 4.0, code MIT. Summaries under 8 sentences and pairs flagged as direct translations are dropped.
method: Three contrasts per story: German original against its supplied English translation (language only); English summary against the translated German summary (retelling only); English against German original (both). Units: those stable across language on the development split. Cross-model link: a ridge map (a regularised linear fit) from development stories; UN21 twins second. A hard gallery uses same-genre, same-decade stories.
rivals: TF-IDF on the supplied English translations (machine translation makes words a rival again), multilingual sentence embeddings, an LLM asked whether two summaries tell one story (500 pairs), length difference, random units, and each model's mean-pooled residual stream. Multilingual embeddings will probably win. The result still shows whether unit agreement exists once shared vocabulary is gone.
premise: Both. Agreement that survives translation would be the first cross-model evidence that is not names and words. A collapse means the study's agreement was lexical, and translation-proof memes need directions or embeddings. Replaces the deferred Chinese protocol with human-written text in languages Llama 3.1 lists as supported.
bio: Synonymous codons: different sequence, same protein.
cost: M. About a week: a data loader, name replacement for the non-English originals, five to ten hours of extraction for two models, no paid API because translations are supplied.
payoff: An answer to Mike's fuzziness question at story scale: retelling, translation and name removal are separated in one natural corpus of thousands of stories instead of 32 works. French, Italian and Spanish repeat the German result.
risk: Both models have read these pages in every language and may simply recognise the film, so stories neither model can name are scored separately. Language editions tell different parts of a story. Leftover names, numbers and cognates (words with a shared root) can leak, and translation errors can hide signal.
review: Defined the unit choice, replaced the dependence on UN21 twins with a fitted map, fixed an impossible gallery and added a recognition check. Dataset confirmed. Remaining: the supplied name-replaced texts are probably English only, and language-general middle layers within one model are already reported (Anthropic 2025).
sources: Hatzel and Biemann 2024 (Tell Me Again, LREC-COLING); Wendler et al. 2024; Anthropic 2025 (On the Biology of a Large Language Model); preregistration/translation_protocol.md

title: Carrying a reading from Qwen into Llama's catalogue
question: Can a tale read by Qwen be matched against a library of tales read by Llama, using a map fitted only on unrelated film text?
hypothesis: Carried by a ridge map (a regularised linear fit) fitted on film sentences, Qwen's readings of name-masked tales find same-type tales in Llama's library with 80% or more of the above-chance precision Llama reaches when it reads the queries itself. Single twins keep under 50%.
falsifier: The ridge-carried reading keeps under 50% of Llama's own above-chance precision, or does no better than a map fitted on misaligned sentences (sign-flip test across 81 tale types; about 80% power for a 0.03 gap if type differences vary by 0.1). Then a catalogue cannot be shared by mapping.
data: Annotated Folktales in the `trilogy` repository (Hagedorn and Darányi, Zenodo 6575263; the repository states CC BY-SA 4.0): 1,518 English tales, each given one of 182 Aarne-Thompson-Uther tale types by the folklorist D. L. Ashliman. Without 20 tales marked non-commercial, 81 types have 8 or more tellings (1,066 tales): the test set. Types with 4 to 7 tellings are for development.
method: Each name-masked tale is read as in the study (top sentences per unit) and as a mid-depth residual-stream vector (the state passed between layers). Qwen's reading is carried into Llama's coordinates by single twins, a 10-unit lasso, full-layer ridge, a rotation, or anchor similarities with no fitting. Statistic: average precision of same-type retrieval. Null: maps fitted on misaligned sentences.
rivals: TF-IDF similarity (needs no map), a sentence-embedding model, an LLM asked whether two tales share a type (subsample), tale length, random units carried the same way, and Llama's pooled residual stream reading the queries itself. TF-IDF is most dangerous; if it wins on precision, retention still settles whether maps work. Same-type pairs with low word overlap are scored separately.
premise: P2. Retention by ridge but not by twins supports P2 restated as shared directions and makes one catalogue practical. Low retention by every map means one catalogue per model, which is Mike's fallback of a single reference model.
bio: Lifting gene annotations from one genome to another.
cost: S. Under an hour of extraction for both models (tales capped at 40 sentences); maps and retrieval in a day or two on the laptop; LLM reading on a subsample.
payoff: How much of a reading survives a change of model, for each kind of map, and whether a meme travels as one neuron, a few neurons or a direction. Readings of texts that cannot be redistributed could then be shared and used with another model.
risk: Tale types share key nouns (hare, slipper), so TF-IDF may sit near the ceiling and leave the maps little room to differ. A film-fitted map may fail on nineteenth-century folktale prose because the text differs, not the models; a map fitted on development tales measures that. Both models have probably read these tales.
review: Rebuilt as retrieval. Picking a detector from 900,000 units on four tellings would overfit, as the study's Qwen revenge unit did; now no unit is chosen on tale labels. Counts confirmed from the file. Remaining: labels come from one folklorist, and tale types may be too lexical.
sources: Hagedorn and Darányi 2022 (Zenodo 6575263); Chen et al. 2025 (model stitching); Moschella et al. 2023; Oozeer et al. 2025

title: Precision and size ladder within Qwen3
question: How much does a unit's reading change with weight precision and model size, compared with the change between model families?
hypothesis: Between 4-bit and 8-bit Qwen3-8B, the same unit's sentence responses correlate at a median of 0.95 or more, and work-level presence agrees at kappa 0.9 or more (agreement corrected for chance). Secondary: the share of units with beyond-word Llama twins (UN21) rises with size from Qwen3-0.6B to 14B, rank correlation 0.9 or more.
falsifier: Presence kappa between 4-bit and 8-bit is under 0.8 for meme units, close to the 0.73 found between Qwen and Llama for the 31 named memes (`nulls.json`). Secondary: the rank correlation of twin share with size is under 0.9 (five sizes reach 0.9 by chance about 1 time in 24). Sample: 25,925 sentences in 1,114 works.
data: The committed study corpus (114 works, 3,700 sentences, original and name-free) and the 1,000 committed random film plots (22,225 sentences); Wikipedia text, CC BY-SA. Models: open Qwen3 weights at 0.6B, 1.7B, 4B, 8B and 14B (Apache 2.0, confirmed on Hugging Face), at 4-bit, 8-bit and 16-bit precision wherever they fit in 24 GB.
method: Precision arm: one unit index read at two precisions on the same text, so wording cannot differ; sentence correlation, presence kappa, whether the 56 core and 31 named memes are selected again, and the same for the 8-bit storage of activations. Size arm: UN21's held-out census between each Qwen3 size and Llama. Nulls: rate-matched unit pairs; misaligned sentences.
rivals: TF-IDF and text length do not change with precision (kappa 1), so they set the ceiling. The mean-pooled residual stream goes through the same comparison and is most dangerous: if it is stable where single units are not, the unit basis is the fragile part. Random non-meme units show whether meme units are more or less stable than average.
premise: Both. Stable readings mean the 4-bit study stands as measured; unstable ones mean every published unit number carries unmeasured noise, and no cross-model agreement can exceed that ceiling. A twin share that grows with size supports convergence with scale; a flat one sides with Koepke et al. against it.
cost: S. An hour or two of extraction per model and precision. The 14B model at 4 bits is the largest that fits beside its activations; the 8B model at 16 bits (about 16 GB) may not fit, but 1.7B and 4B at 16 bits do.
payoff: A reliability figure for the instrument itself, which the study never measured, and a ceiling against which every cross-model agreement number can be read.
risk: The likely result is dull: readings are stable, which is still worth knowing. Unit indices line up across precisions but not across sizes, so the size arm inherits every weakness of twin matching, has one model per size, and Llama's fixed 8B size may favour the 8B Qwen whatever the trend.
review: Made precision the primary arm and size a stated secondary with its own small-sample test; dropped the claim that this tests whether neurons are clean. All checkpoints confirmed. Remaining: five sizes with one model each cannot separate scale from similarity to Llama's own size.
sources: Cammarata 2026; Huh et al. 2024; Koepke et al. 2026; study/results/robustness/nulls.json

title: Shared units against human judgements of similarity
question: Do the units two models share predict which texts people judge alike better than the units only one model has?
hypothesis: Across sentence pairs rated by people, distance over shared units tracks the human score better than distance over model-specific units, by 0.05 or more in rank correlation after word overlap and length are removed. On story triples, shared units pick the story the annotators chose more often.
falsifier: The gap in partial rank correlation is under 0.02, or the shared-unit term adds nothing once word overlap is in the regression (p above 0.05). 8,628 pairs give a standard error near 0.01. The 1,039 story triples can only detect a gap of 5 to 6 points, so they cannot refute alone.
data: STS Benchmark (Cer et al. 2017): 8,628 English sentence pairs with human similarity scores; no licence is stated on its dataset card, so confirm it and commit ids only. SemEval-2026 Task 4 (Hatzel et al. 2026): 1,039 story-summary triples with human choices (200 development, 800 test); confirm the licence on the task site before registering.
method: Qwen and Llama read each text. Shared units pass UN21's held-out, beyond-word twin test. Model-specific units have no twin and are matched on layer, firing rate, word-predictability and stability across precision (UN24). Statistics: partial rank correlation of unit distance with the human score; triple accuracy; both repeated where word overlap and the human score disagree. Null: random unit sets.
rivals: Word overlap and TF-IDF, a general sentence embedding (trained on such data, it will win outright), an LLM asked directly (subsample), length difference, random units, and each model's pooled residual stream, the dangerous one for units. The design still shows whether cross-model agreement marks the part of a reading people share.
premise: P2, and the bridge to readers. A pass supports the convergence argument: what models agree on is what people see, so twin strength could filter for real memes. A fail means cross-model agreement and human relevance are separate properties, so universality cannot stand in for human validation.
bio: Sequence conserved across species as a sign of function.
cost: S. Short texts, two extraction passes, archived human labels, no new raters. Needs the unit lists from UN21 and UN24 first.
payoff: The first check of any unit reading in this project against human judgement, at no rater cost, and a test of whether twin strength is a useful filter for memes people would recognise.
risk: Sentence pairs from captions and headlines are far from story memes. The story triples are few, were kept only where two LLMs disagreed, and annotators agreed weakly (alpha 0.33). Units without twins may simply be noisier, which matching can only partly remove.
review: The story triples alone were fatal: 1,039 in all, kept only where LLMs disagree, annotator agreement 0.33, best system 78%. Added 8,628 rated sentence pairs for power and a stability-matched control. Remaining: depends on UN21 and UN24, and sentence similarity is not story similarity.
sources: Cer et al. 2017 (STS Benchmark); Hatzel et al. 2026 (SemEval-2026 Task 4); Huh et al. 2024; Marti et al. 2023

title: Text-chosen units read from pixels in one model
question: Does a unit that responds to a scene described in words respond to the same scene shown as an image with no lettering?
hypothesis: In Qwen3-VL-8B, 30% or more of units that agree across two people's captions of an image (correlation 0.5 or more) also agree between caption and pixels at 0.3 or more on unseen images, against under 5% for mismatched unit pairs.
falsifier: Under 10% of caption-reliable units transfer to pixels, or no more than mismatched unit pairs matched on firing rate, or transfer vanishes on images with no detected lettering. Then unit readings are bound to text. 1,800 held-out images give a per-unit correlation standard error near 0.024.
data: Crossmodal-3600 (Thapliyal et al. 2022): 3,600 photographs from around the world with human captions in 36 languages, written independently and not translated; captions CC BY 4.0 (17 MB), images 302 MB with an attribution file. Half the images to choose units, half to score. Typographic decoys (a caption rendered as an image) are generated.
method: Model: Qwen3-VL-8B at 4 bits, whose language layers have the same shape as the study's Qwen3-8B; first measure whether a unit index gives the same reading of text in both. Read every unit on caption tokens with no image, and on image tokens with a neutral prompt. Per unit: caption-to-caption, caption-to-pixel and caption-to-decoy correlation. Nulls: mismatched unit pairs; shuffled images.
rivals: In one task, finding an image's own caption among 1,800: text-chosen units reading pixels against a contrastive image-text model (CLIP or SigLIP), the model's own written caption matched by TF-IDF, its pooled residual stream, and image brightness and size as the analogue of length. CLIP will win retrieval; the transfer share still says whether a text catalogue reads images.
premise: P1 mainly, P2 across media. Transfer means units pass the concept-cell test of invariance (one response to a word and a picture), which name detectors fail. No transfer means one catalogue per medium, and the poster experiment cannot be joined to the text study.
bio: Concept cells that fire to a face and its written name.
cost: M. New extraction code for a vision-language model, then a few hours of compute for 3,600 images and their captions.
payoff: Whether one catalogue can read both text and images, whether the study's own Qwen3-8B units carry over to pictures, and a controlled replacement for the poster experiment, which had no cheap rival and no lettering control.
risk: Captions describe concrete scenes, so a pass shows invariance for objects and places, the easy case, and says little about story memes such as revenge or a secret identity. A model trained to caption images may fire word units on pixels simply because it is about to write the word.
review: Switched to Qwen3-VL-8B (checkpoint confirmed; same layer count and widths as Qwen3-8B) so the study's own units can be tested, and put the rivals into one retrieval task. Remaining: units shared between text and image are already reported for such models, and photographs are far from story memes.
sources: Thapliyal et al. 2022 (Crossmodal-3600); Goh et al. 2021; Quian Quiroga et al. 2005; Schwettmann et al. 2023

title: Steered in Qwen, read in Llama
question: When Qwen is steered to write a meme with its usual words blocked, does the matching Llama unit detect it in the text?
hypothesis: For 100 Qwen units with beyond-word twins, passages written under steering (the unit's activation raised during writing) are traced to the right unit by Llama's twin readings at 20% top-1 or better (chance 1%), and at half or more of that rate when each unit's ten best words are banned from the output.
falsifier: Top-1 is under 5% with words banned, or no better than for matched Qwen units that lack a beyond-word twin, steered the same way. Then twin agreement does not survive when the meme is set by intervention. 100 units by 20 passages give 2,000 trials and a standard error under 1 point.
data: Generated by the experiment, no outside data: for each of 100 Qwen3-8B units (from UN21's list and the study's labelled concept units), 20 short story continuations from neutral prompts with the unit raised, the same for 100 matched comparison units, and unsteered controls. About 6,000 passages of 60 words, released under CC BY 4.0.
method: Ground truth: which unit was raised. Qwen writes; Llama only reads. Each passage is assigned to the unit whose Llama twin responds most, scaled by the unsteered controls. Word ban: the unit's ten best words (UN21's lasso) cannot be output. Steering strength is set on separate development units, and a blind LLM check confirms the text stays fluent.
rivals: Given half the passages for training: a TF-IDF classifier, a sentence-embedding classifier, and an LLM reader shown the unit labels. Also word overlap with each unit's top sentences, passage length, and Llama's pooled residual stream. TF-IDF is most dangerous without the ban, the embedding classifier with it. Twins get no training passages, so a tie favours twins.
premise: Both. The only test in this area where the meme in a text is known by construction. A pass shows a unit means the same thing when written by one model and read by another. A fail alongside a pass in UN21 means twins share inputs, not meaning.
bio: A gene moved into another species and still expressed there.
cost: S to M. A steering hook is a few lines in the existing recorder (`study/extract.py`); about five hours of generation on the laptop, minutes of reading, and a small LLM check.
payoff: Causal evidence for or against P2 at unit level, and the first steering result of any kind in this project. Cammarata's essay uses steering as the direct test of a unit's label, and the study never ran it.
risk: Units that read a concept often do not write it, and raising a single unit in a 4-bit 8B model may produce nothing or nonsense; the share of steerable units is itself a result. With words banned, steering may fail outright, leaving nothing for Llama to read.
review: Added: no design in the area had a causal check, and this seed was the only one with ground truth set by intervention. Remaining weakness: single-unit steering may fail on most units, and steering transfer between models by learned maps is already reported (Agarwal 2026), though not this reading test.
sources: Cammarata 2026; Oozeer et al. 2025; Agarwal 2026; study/extract.py

title: Crosscoder latents against neurons on heredity
question: Do the shared latents of a joint Qwen-Llama dictionary recover documented sources on name-free text beyond words, where Qwen's neurons failed?
note: A crosscoder is one sparse dictionary that reads both models. Jiralerspong and Bricken 2026 trained one on this exact pair and say the training code is public; released weights were not confirmed, so budget 2 to 5 GPU days. Rivals: TF-IDF, word presence and sentence embeddings in the same residual test. Standard crosscoders lean towards calling features shared (Minder et al. 2025).

title: Mapped revenge direction
question: If Llama's revenge direction is carried into Qwen by a paired linear map, does Qwen detect revenge without the word, where its own unit scored 4 of 12?
note: Uses the 12 committed minimal pairs (`study/results/wording.json`) plus about 200 new ones checked by hand. Rivals: a sentence-embedding prototype and an LLM yes/no. One day on the laptop.

title: Trilingual brain check
question: Do units shared across models explain brain responses to one story heard in English, Chinese and French beyond word rate, position and static word embeddings?
note: Le Petit Prince fMRI corpus (Li et al. 2022, Scientific Data 9:530, public). Use contiguous train-test splits, as Feghhi et al. and Hadidi et al. require. Guo et al. 2026 already report sparse-autoencoder features of Llama-3.1-8B against brain data in these three languages, so the new part is cross-model units and the word-level controls. Expect a null; needs someone who knows fMRI encoding models. Cost M to L.

title: Does universality select for words?
question: How much of the variation in twin strength is explained by how word-like a unit is?
note: Hours, no model runs: per-unit fields are committed for 71 memes, not 200 (`study/results/robustness/nulls.json`, `f2_agreement/per_meme`); the rest need exporting. Rival predictor: best-word correlation alone. If it explains most of twin strength, twin strength is a poor filter for real memes.

title: Third family and second checkpoint
question: Is Qwen-Llama agreement typical of any two models, or does it change with a third family or a second checkpoint of one family?
note: Separates shared training text from convergence. The study found Qwen3-1.7B agreed with Qwen3-8B no better than Llama did (median 0.40 in both, `study/results/phylo.json.gz`). Gemma or Mistral at 4 bits fit the laptop. Same held-out and word-matched nulls as UN21.

title: Where the two models disagree
question: Are the units with no twin in the other model concentrated in culturally or politically loaded content?
note: Jiralerspong and Bricken 2026 report Chinese-state-aligned features exclusive to Qwen3-8B and American-exceptionalism features exclusive to Llama. Compare twinless units on neutral plots against history or news text. Rival: topic words. Tells users when the choice of reference model matters.

title: Story memes in generated scenes
question: Does one unit fire for a story meme stated in text and shown in a generated image with decoys and masked lettering?
note: Follow-up to UN26 for narrative memes such as a secret identity. Ground truth by construction, with a human check of a sample. Rivals: CLIP zero-shot, a captioner plus TF-IDF, the model asked directly.

title: Two languages, one photograph, no translator
question: Do units agree between English and German captions that two people wrote separately for the same photograph?
note: Crossmodal-3600 has captions written independently in 36 languages for 3,600 images (CC BY 4.0). A check on UN22 that is free of machine-translation artefacts, with Qwen reading German against Llama reading English as the cross-model step. Rivals: multilingual sentence embeddings, TF-IDF after translation, caption length. Concrete scenes only. Hours.

title: Scrambled sentences
question: How much twin agreement survives when the words of each sentence are shuffled, so that only the bag of words is left?
note: Reread UN21's film sentences with word order shuffled inside each sentence. Agreement that survives is carried by vocabulary alone; the drop is the share that needs word order. A check on UN21's word control that fits no model. Rival: TF-IDF, which shuffling leaves unchanged. Under a day.

title: Scientific memes along citations, with shared words controlled
question: Does a paper carry the neuron units of a paper it cites more than those of an uncited paper whose wording is just as close?
hypothesis: On held-out pairs where an uncited same-year decoy is matched to the cited paper on TF-IDF similarity (word overlap weighted by rarity; within 0.02), units pick the cited paper at least 60% of the time (chance 50%), and at least 2 points more often than random units with the same firing rate.
falsifier: Unit accuracy under 55%, or within 1 point of random units, on 20,000 held-out pairs from at least 4,000 citing papers (standard error roughly 0.5 points when resampled by citing paper). A second failure after Batman would settle that neurons add nothing to words for descent.
data: SNAP cit-HepTh: 27,770 physics papers with abstracts and all 352,807 citation links among them, 1993 to 2003 (checked 2026-11-08; no licence stated, so commit only IDs). Second field: about 30,000 biomedical abstracts with links from OpenAlex (CC0 per its documentation; needs a free key, anonymous access was refused on 2026-11-08).
method: Unit: a feed-forward neuron (Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen3 8B), present when it fires strongly. Re-derive Kuhn's propagation score for units and n-grams. Pick the 2,000 best-propagating units on early links. On later links between papers unseen in tuning, sharing no author, count units shared with the cited paper and with the decoy. Repeat without word-detector units. Null: time-preserving link shuffle.
rivals: TF-IDF and BM25 (near 50% by design), Kuhn's n-gram score, a general sentence embedding, a citation-trained embedding (SPECTER2) as ceiling, an LLM reading both abstracts on 2,000 pairs, length, random units, the model's averaged internal state. The general embedding is most dangerous: popular ones were themselves trained on citation pairs. If it wins, units are not needed for descent.
premise: P1. A pass is the first evidence on natural text at scale that units follow inherited ideas past the wording. A fail, added to Batman, leaves P1 without practical content for descent. Agreement between the two models bears weakly on P2.
cost: M. About 400,000 sentences, a few hours per model on a laptop; most of the two weeks goes on assembling links and matching decoys.
payoff: Whether Kuhn's finding survives word matching when it is measured in units, and a reusable heredity benchmark with tens of thousands of documented links, the scale Batman lacked.
risk: A citation is weak evidence that an idea was inherited; most references are background. Matching on TF-IDF leaves shared subtopic; a second decoy set, co-cited with the source by a third paper, tests that. Close decoys exist mainly for loosely related citations, so the test pairs may not be typical.
review: Added a closed, key-free corpus (cit-HepTh) so Kuhn's score can be re-derived; split by paper, dropped shared-author pairs, added random-unit and co-cited-decoy checks. Remaining: a citation is weak evidence of inheritance, and embeddings trained on citation pairs will probably beat units.
sources: Kuhn, Perc and Helbing 2014 (arXiv:1404.3757); SNAP cit-HepTh; OpenAlex; Edmonds 2002, Three challenges for the survival of memetics

title: Sperber's test: are retold ideas copied or rebuilt
question: When a story is retold down a chain, is its new content a copying error passed on to later retellings, or something each chain adds independently because every teller rebuilds the story the same way?
hypothesis: The memetic prediction: of the units a story gains by step 8, those inherited from the chain's own step 4 and absent from sibling chains outnumber those that also arose in sibling chains by at least 2 to 1. A step-8 retelling is matched to its own step-4 ancestor among six siblings at least 50% of the time (chance 17%).
falsifier: A copied-to-rebuilt ratio of 1 or less, with a bootstrap interval lying below 2, in both reader models, over 360 test chains from 60 stories (resampled by story; E3 had 15 works) and at least 2,000 gains; or matching under 30%. That is Sperber's outcome: new content is convergent, so shared units cannot be read as descent.
data: Built for the test and released with its lineage. 80 new 300-word stories without proper names, written from randomly drawn plot elements (20 for tuning, 60 for scoring). Each starts 6 chains that share only the seed. A chain is 8 retellings of about 150 words by two small open models taking turns, not the reader models: 3,840 texts.
method: Readers: Qwen3 8B, Llama 3.1 8B; presence rule set on tuning stories. A gain is a unit absent from the seed and from the story's first retellings, present at step 8, and rare elsewhere (not house style). Copied: also in the chain's own step 4, in no sibling. Rebuilt: in a sibling's step 8. Null: chain labels shuffled within story.
rivals: The same count on content words and on LLM-listed plot points; sentence embeddings, text length, random units and the mean-pooled residual stream for the matching test only. The LLM plot-point list is most dangerous. The ratio is a result about transmission whichever tool gives it; units earn a place only if a human check of 200 gains favours them.
premise: P1. Also bears on how E2 is read. A ratio above 2 answers Sperber for these tellers. A ratio below 1 means resemblance in retold culture is largely convergence, so a neuron-defined meme would measure a shared attractor and not a lineage.
bio: Parallel evolution in replicate lines; homoplasy against shared descent
cost: M. About 3,900 short texts from local 4-bit models, one to two days of laptop time, plus two reading passes and one LLM plot-point pass.
payoff: A number for how much of what a retold story gains is inherited and how much is rebuilt, plus a list of convergent units to exclude from later lineage tests.
risk: Model tellers are not human minds, and the retelling prompt sets how faithfully they copy, so the ratio is a fact about these tellers. Small models may add little, leaving too few gains. Dropped details are not counted, because selection and attraction predict the same losses.
review: The original ratio depended on how profiles were centred and counted house style as attraction. Replaced with six replicate chains per story and a count of inherited gains against gains that recur in sibling chains. Remaining: model tellers, a prompt that sets fidelity, and no human chains yet.
sources: Sperber 2000; Claidière, Scott-Phillips and Sperber 2014; Perez et al. 2024 (arXiv:2407.04503); Acerbi and Stubbersfield 2023

title: Silent and loud mutations in copied news quotes
question: When a news quote changes by one word as it is copied, can neuron units tell meaning-keeping changes from meaning-changing ones, and are the meaning-changing versions reused less often?
hypothesis: On 600 hand-labelled natural swaps, the change in pre-chosen units separates silent swaps (meaning kept) from loud ones (meaning changed) with an AUC of at least 0.75 (0.5 is chance), within 0.05 of sentence-embedding similarity. Loud versions are then reused by another site at most 80% as often as silent ones.
falsifier: AUC under 0.65, or more than 0.05 below embeddings (standard error about 0.02). For spread: with at least 3,000 swaps, 500 of them loud, a loud-to-silent reuse ratio above 0.95 whose 95% interval excludes 0.8. With fewer swaps the spread test is declared uninformative, not passed.
data: MemeTracker phrase clusters (SNAP; one 220 MB file, reachable 2026-11-08; August 2008 to April 2009; no licence stated, so commit only IDs and derived numbers). One-word swaps mined with Lerique and Roth's method (code GPLv3); the number of swaps is unknown until mined. 800 swaps labelled by hand, 150 of them twice. Tuning pairs built from WordNet synonyms and antonyms.
method: Pairs share every word but one, so word overlap cannot separate them. Drop tense, number and spelling changes. Choose units on built pairs (synonym swap silent, antonym swap loud) and 200 labelled swaps; score on 600. The best tool labels all swaps; compare reuse by a later, different site within parent quote and week. Null: labels shuffled within parent.
rivals: Edit distance (constant by design), WordNet synonymy and word-vector similarity of the two swapped words, sentence-embedding similarity, an LLM judging both versions, random units, the mean-pooled residual stream. The LLM judge is most likely to win. The silent-to-loud split and the spread test then run on its labels and still give memetics a fidelity figure.
premise: P1. A pass shows units respond to meaning in natural minimal pairs, where the study had 31 hand-made rewordings. A fail says units are too coarse for short texts. The spread result says whether meaning is protected in copying; Atran and the memeticists both expect that, so it does not separate them.
cost: M. Model time is under a day because quotes are short; mining the swaps and hand-labelling 800 pairs take about three days for one person.
payoff: A first copying-fidelity figure for ideas as opposed to strings: what share of copying errors is silent, and whether meaning-changing errors are weeded out.
risk: Most MemeTracker variants are truncations, so clean one-word swaps may number only a few thousand. Which version is the parent is inferred from timing, not documented. A loud change may be the correction of a misquote, which would spread more and hide selection.
review: Replaced PAWS (word-order pairs, the wrong kind) with built synonym and antonym swaps; changed the spread outcome to reuse by another site and said when it is uninformative. Remaining: an LLM judge will win the labelling, swap counts are unknown, and parent direction is inferred.
sources: Leskovec, Backstrom and Kleinberg 2009 (MemeTracker); Lerique and Roth 2018; Simmons, Adamic and Adar 2011; Atran 2001

title: Heylighen's selection criteria on randomised headline tests
question: Do the criteria that Heylighen (1998) says help a meme get noticed and accepted, scored by neuron units chosen in advance, predict which headline wins a randomised test?
hypothesis: On confirmatory tests, at least 4 of 6 criteria (distinctiveness, novelty, simplicity, authority, formality, utility) raise click rate with 95% intervals excluding zero, and together they add at least 2 points of winner accuracy over headline length and punctuation.
falsifier: Fewer than 3 of 6 criteria significant in the predicted direction, or under 1 added point, on at least 5,000 confirmatory tests where only the headline differs (standard error about 0.7 points). Separately, units fail if LLM ratings of the same criteria beat them by more than 1 point.
data: Upworthy Research Archive (OSF jd64p, CC BY 4.0): 32,487 randomised tests, 150,817 arms, 2013 to 2015. Drop tests the archive's own column flags for unreliable randomisation (about 22%); keep tests where only the headline differs (count not yet checked). Tune on its exploratory part, score once on its confirmatory part. Archived data; nothing is optimised on a live audience.
method: Use only criteria Heylighen assigns to assimilation (being noticed, understood, accepted), which a click measures. For each, write 80 contrast pairs (same content, criterion high or low); pick units on 60, check on 20, freeze. No click data chooses units. Within each test, criterion differences predict the winner (conditional logistic regression), controlling length and punctuation. Null: arms shuffled within test.
rivals: An LLM rating each headline 1 to 7 on each criterion, readability and word-rarity formulas, an embedding probe trained on the contrast pairs, word n-grams, sparse-autoencoder features (Movva et al. 2025), random units, the mean-pooled residual stream. The LLM rater is most dangerous, because the criteria are defined in words. If it wins, the criteria still get a signed test.
premise: P1. If unit-scored criteria predict as well as LLM ratings, units measure abstract properties of a meme and not only words. If only the ratings work, the theory survives without the unit. If neither works, the criteria fail at the attention stage.
cost: M. 150,000 headlines take an hour or two per model; rating six criteria with a local LLM takes about a day.
payoff: The first test of Heylighen's assimilation criteria as a signed set on randomised data, and a check of whether units chosen in advance can stand in for a reader's rating.
risk: Simplicity is already known to win on this archive (Shulman et al. 2024), so one criterion is a replication. Heylighen himself hedges on formality. Contrast pairs written by an LLM may differ in style as well as in the criterion. Click-bait habits may swamp the rest.
review: Cut to the six criteria Heylighen assigns to assimilation; expressivity and proselytism belong to later stages. Removed an unsourced count of flagged tests. Simplicity is already published on this archive (Shulman et al. 2024). Remaining: LLM ratings will probably tie the units.
sources: Heylighen 1998; Matias et al. 2021 (Upworthy Research Archive); Shulman, Markowitz and Rogers 2024; Movva et al. 2025 (arXiv:2502.04382)

title: Do reposted ideas wear out beyond their words
question: When an image is reposted to Reddit under a new title, does repeating the idea of an earlier title cost votes even when no words are shared?
hypothesis: Among reposts sharing no content word with earlier titles of the image, similarity in units to earlier titles lowers vote rank by at least 1.5 percentile points more (most against least similar third) than similarity to later titles, which cannot cause fatigue. The penalty is larger when the earlier post was in the same subreddit.
falsifier: An earlier-minus-later gap under 0.5 points, or of the wrong sign, on at least 20,000 reposts that have both earlier and later titles (standard error about 0.5 points, resampled by image). Units also fail if the gap disappears once sentence-embedding similarity is added to the model.
data: SNAP Reddit submissions (Lakkaraju et al. 2013): 132,308 posts of 16,736 images, July 2008 to January 2013, one 7.6 MB CSV. Counted on the file on 2026-11-08: 53,515 reposts share no content word with any earlier title, and 46,201 of those also have a later title. No licence stated, so commit only IDs and derived features.
method: First re-derive the published word-based title effect; units must reproduce it on reposts that share words. Outcome: vote rank within subreddit and month, adjusted for hour, repost number and days since the last post (a content-free baseline, after Weng). Predictor: similarity to earlier titles, and to later titles as placebo, in units, words and embeddings. Tune on 30% of images.
rivals: Word overlap (zero by design), sentence-embedding similarity, an LLM asked whether two titles make the same point, title length, random units, the mean-pooled residual stream. Embeddings are most dangerous. If they win, idea fatigue is still shown beyond words, which is Coscia's claim under control, and the unit is not needed for it.
premise: P1. A penalty that units detect where words cannot would show units following a short idea through rewording in wild data. A null or an embedding tie leaves P1 where Batman left it.
cost: S. 132,000 short titles, under an hour per model, and a day of analysis.
payoff: Whether competition for attention acts on ideas or on strings, and an answer to whether similar memes help or hurt each other with the content held fixed.
risk: Titles are short (median 5 words, counted on the file) and describe an image the model never sees, so unit profiles may be mostly noise. A title close to earlier ones may only be a plain description; the later-title placebo removes that only if plain titles are as common early as late.
review: Made the later-title placebo the test statistic and added a same-subreddit contrast, because closeness to earlier titles may only mark a plain description. Confirmed 53,515 eligible reposts on the file. Remaining: titles have a median of 5 words, so unit profiles may be noise.
sources: Lakkaraju, McAuley and Leskovec 2013; Coscia 2014; Weng et al. 2012

title: Do memes survive retelling better in bundles
question: Does a story element survive a chain of retellings more often when its usual partner element is in the story than when an unrelated element takes the partner's place?
hypothesis: After four retellings an element survives at least 10 percentage points more often in a whole bundle than in a broken one, the gap is positive in at least 17 of 24 bundles, and a neutral filler element shows less than half that gap.
falsifier: A gap under 3 points, or a 95% interval (resampled by bundle) that includes zero, over 1,440 chains from 480 seed stories (standard error about 3.5 points). That would mean elements are lost one by one, and the memeplex adds nothing to its parts in transmission.
data: Built for the test. 24 two-element bundles fixed in advance (such as orphan plus revenge vow), from the trope pairs that co-occur most in the TV Tropes tables of Gala et al. 2020 (pair list only; the site's licence is non-commercial). Each gets 10 outlines, written whole and broken: 480 name-free 300-word stories, 3 chains of 4 retellings, 5,760 texts.
method: A memeplex is a set of memes said to help each other spread. A coin flip decides whether the partner is present, so topic cannot explain the gap. Survival at the last step is read by units chosen on separate planted-element stories and checked against 400 human-labelled retellings. Statistic: survival in whole minus broken stories, paired by outline.
rivals: A keyword list for each element, an embedding probe, an LLM reader asked whether the element is present, text length, random units, the mean-pooled residual stream. The LLM reader is most dangerous, and the keyword list will win for elements with an obvious word. If either wins, the bundle effect is still the first randomised test of co-adapted memes.
premise: P1. The bundle effect itself does not depend on the unit. Units earn a place only if units chosen on planted stories track an element through four rewordings as accurately as the LLM reader, judged against the human labels.
cost: M. About 6,500 short texts from local 4-bit models, two to three days of laptop time, plus half a day labelling 400 retellings.
payoff: A causal number for whether memes in a complex protect each other in transmission, and a list of bundles that behave as larger units.
risk: Model tellers are not human minds, and four short retellings may keep everything (chain length is set on tuning stories). Memory research already shows that causally linked events are recalled better (Trabasso and van den Broek 1985), so a pass may be old news under a new name.
review: The citation version could not fail: units that co-fire inside the model, and words in set phrases, stay linked whatever culture does. Rewritten as a randomised test of whether a partner element protects an element in retelling. Remaining: model tellers; memory research partly predicts the result.
sources: Dawkins 1976; Blackmore 1999; Trabasso and van den Broek 1985; Gala et al. 2020 (TV Tropes dataset)

title: Know Your Meme family tree
question: Does a meme entry carry the units of its documented parent meme more than those of unrelated memes?
note: IMKG (Tommasini et al. 2023) and the Zannettou et al. 2018 Zenodo set hold the links. Hosting, licence and scraping terms are unchecked. Captions follow templates, so word overlap will probably win; the images need vision neurons.

title: Dennett's grain size
question: At what unit size (single neuron, merged family, sentence, document) does heredity along citations peak, and does the curve differ from the one for unigram, bigram and phrase?
note: Reuses ME21's data. A flat curve, or one that tracks the n-gram curve, means there is no natural meme size.

title: Edmonds' Challenge 1, items 4 and 5
question: Do unit frequencies across generations of papers show a non-zero selection term in a Price-equation split, against a content-free limited-attention simulation?
note: Weng et al. 2012 supplies the null; the rival is the same split on n-grams. Analysis only once ME21 exists.

title: The 1997 learned unit, side by side
question: Do Pocklington and Best's latent-semantic term clusters match neuron units on ME21's word-matched citation test?
note: A learned unit was tried 29 years ago and changed nothing. If it ties neurons here, the instrument was not what memetics lacked.

title: Memorable against forgotten movie lines
question: Do Heylighen's criteria, scored by the units frozen in ME24, pick the memorable quote over a matched line by the same speaker in the same scene?
note: Danescu-Niculescu-Mizil et al. 2012. The Cornell data page failed with a certificate error again on 2026-11-08, so hosting is unconfirmed. The rival is their word-rarity model. It would cover the retention stage, which ME24 cannot.

title: Lynch's pass-it-on unit
question: Is there a unit for 'urge the reader to pass this on', and does it predict copy number in chain letters or copy-pasted posts?
note: No public cascade data found: Adamic et al.'s Facebook data is closed and the chain-letter archive was unreachable. A keyword list is the rival and will be hard to beat.

title: Sperber's test on human chains
question: Does ME22's copied-to-rebuilt ratio hold when people do the retelling, and how much of what survives is explained by the receiver and not the source (Gabora)?
note: Breithaupt et al. 2018 ran 285 human chains of three retellings, but on only three base stories, and whether the retelling texts are public is unconfirmed (one supplementary file). Needed before ME22 says anything about people.

title: Copy the product or the instructions
question: Do chains that regenerate a story from an outline keep more units than chains that paraphrase the finished text, as Blackmore claims?
note: Blackmore's distinction is confirmed; which mode she ranks as more faithful is from memory. Rival: content-word retention. A cheap extra arm for ME22.

title: Linkage along citations (was ME26)
question: Are pairs of units passed from a cited paper to a citing paper together more often than their separate rates predict?
note: Demoted. Units that co-fire inside the model and words in set phrases would stay linked across periods whatever culture does, and a shared subtopic gives the same pattern. It needs pairs with no background association before it can fail.

title: A mutation rate per retelling
question: What share of units is lost or gained at each step of a retelling chain, and is the rate lower for units than for content words?
note: Free once ME22's chains exist. Dawkins's copying fidelity as a number. The rival is the same rate on words and on LLM-listed plot points; a human-chain figure needs the data in the seed above.

title: Citations the paper leans on
question: Does ME21's unit advantage grow for references that the citing paper mentions several times in its full text?
note: Answers ME21's weak ground truth with a dose measure that does not come from the abstracts. Needs open full text with in-text citation counts (the PubMed Central open-access subset that Kuhn used); parsing and coverage are unchecked.

title: Steer the named memes: a causal label test
question: When a labelled meme unit is pushed up while the model writes, do blind judges recover its label, even with the meme's usual words banned?
hypothesis: At one fluent dose per unit, at least 8 of the 31 named Qwen3-8B units pass: judges choose the unit's own label, from 31 plus 'none', on at least half of 20 held-out openings. With the label's words banned from the output, at most 4 still pass, mostly story patterns such as the funeral and the secret identity.
falsifier: Fewer than 4 of 31 units pass, or no more pass than at the 99th percentile when labels are shuffled among the 31 units' texts: then the labels are not causal. More than 4 passes under the ban refutes the word-emitter half. Shuffled labels should give about one pass or fewer, so 31 units are enough.
data: No new corpus. The 31 unit labels fixed in October 2026 (`study/results/labels.json`, MIT). Ban lists fixed before generation: keywords from `preregistration/memes_for_tracing.json`, each unit's 20 most-promoted output words, and character names. 30 neutral story openings written for this test (10 to set doses, 20 held out). Qwen3-8B at 4-bit and 8-bit; Llama 3.1 8B twins as a replication.
method: Steering adds a fixed amount to one unit's activation as the model continues an opening. Each unit keeps the largest of five doses that leaves text at most three times as surprising as normal to the unsteered model. Two LLM judges, checked on 200 blind human ratings, choose a label. Secondary: switch the unit off and ask for the meme.
rivals: The unit's 20 most-promoted output words handed to the same judges with no generated text (most dangerous: if it ties, units emit names, confirming labels as words, not ideas). A prompt that asks for the label (ceiling). A direction built from keyword-matched sentences. 62 random units matched on layer and firing rate, showing how often any push draws a label.
premise: P1. Passes under the keyword ban are the first causal evidence that a unit carries an idea. Passes only without the ban mean units are word emitters. A general fail means the paper's labels describe what units read, not what they do.
bio: Gene overexpression: turn one gene up, look for the trait.
cost: S. One to two days on the laptop, a few dollars of judge calls, two hours of human rating.
payoff: The causal check the paper named as missing, for every showcase meme, and a shortlist of units safe to use as edit handles.
risk: In small 4-bit models the gap between no effect and gibberish is narrow, so many units may fail for dose reasons and the result reads as untested, not refuted.
review: Replaced the invented 5% null with a shuffled-label null, fixed one dose per unit on tuning openings, and fixed ban lists in advance. Remaining weakness: the file tags only 13 of the 31 labels as tropes; 8 are characters, which can hardly pass the ban.
sources: Kran Research 2026, Evil Qwen replication (blog.kran.ai/evil-qwen); Cammarata 2026, Neural networks are already clean; Liu 2026, arXiv:2606.19831; Arad, Mueller, Belinkov 2025, arXiv:2505.20063

title: More A, less B: rewriting against prompting
question: Can any internal handle (one neuron, a direction or a sparse-autoencoder feature) move an existing story toward meme A and away from meme B better than simply asking a model to rewrite it?
hypothesis: No. The prompt-only rewrite gets the highest combined score, and the best internal handle reaches under 80% of it. Among handles, the difference-of-means direction (average activation on texts with the meme minus texts without) does best and the single neuron worst.
falsifier: The handle arm that scored best on the tuning stories, alone or added to the prompt, beats prompt-only by 0.05 or more on the 0-to-1 combined score, with a 95% interval above zero, on 160 held-out stories. That gives about 85% power if per-story differences have a spread of 0.2, less if meme pairs differ a lot.
data: 208 film plots from the CMU Movie Summary Corpus (42,306 Wikipedia summaries, CC BY-SA), skipping the pre-registration's reserved films, cut to 10 sentences, names masked. For each of 16 seeded meme pairs from `preregistration/memes_for_tracing.json`: 13 plots containing B and not A, confirmed by an LLM reader and a human (3 tuning, 10 held out). Llama Scope sparse autoencoders (Apache 2.0).
method: Six arms on Llama 3.1 8B: prompt only; one neuron; 20 neurons; direction; sparse-autoencoder feature (a unit from a separately trained dictionary of activations); prompt plus direction. Handles use EN-23's contrast sentences. A Qwen3-8B judge and blind humans score A up, B down, story kept and fluency, combined so that failing one sinks the score. Repeated with A's keywords banned.
rivals: Prompt-only rewriting, the most dangerous: it beat every activation method on AxBench. Also keyword insertion (paste A's typical words in), a random direction of equal size, and text length. If prompting wins, neurons stay meters and editing tools should be built on prompts scored by the instrument.
premise: P1. A handle that beats prompting shows units are causal levers on meaning, strong support. If prompting wins, P1 survives only as a way to read memes, and meme engineering means prompt and measure.
cost: M. About a week on the laptop, with PyTorch for the feature arm or a small rented GPU; judge calls; four hours of human rating.
payoff: A straight answer on whether to build a meme editor on activations or on prompts, and a benchmark for narrow story motifs, which AxBench does not cover.
risk: A prompt win is the expected result after AxBench, so the news value is modest. Judges may reward stated keywords, so arms look alike. The public sparse autoencoder was trained on the base model; if it rebuilds under 90% of the 4-bit Instruct model's activation variance, that arm is dropped.
review: The 1,000 random films are the paused pre-registration's held-out set, so the data moved to the CMU corpus. Base stories must now contain B, or 'less B' is empty. One pre-chosen handle contrast replaces five. Remaining weakness: a prompt win is already expected.
sources: Wu et al. 2025, AxBench, arXiv:2501.17148; Chen et al. 2025, Persona vectors, arXiv:2507.21509; He et al. 2024, Llama Scope, arXiv:2410.20526; Bamman, O'Connor, Smith 2013, CMU Movie Summary Corpus

title: Do reading units write?
question: Is the unit that best detects a meme in text also the unit that best produces it when pushed?
hypothesis: Mostly not. Across 20 memes, the 10 best detector units and the 10 best writer units share under 20% of their members, and detectors steer successfully less than half as often as writers.
falsifier: Detectors steer as well as writers (success rates within 10 points on held-out prompts), or the two top-10 sets overlap by more than 50%. Twenty memes give about 85% power for a 25-point gap if memes differ with a spread of 35 points. Detectors that steer no better than random units are sensors only.
data: 20 of the 34 meme definitions in `preregistration/memes_for_tracing.json`. For each, 60 LLM-written sentence pairs with and without the meme, its usual words banned, checked by a second model and a 10% human sample: 30 pairs to pick units, 30 held out. The study's own 18 mapped units (`preregistration/dev_units.json`). Qwen3-8B and Llama 3.1 8B open weights.
method: Detectors: units ranked by how well activation separates the pairs. Writers: 2,000 shortlisted units, each pushed on tuning prompts and ranked by the rise in probability of meme sentences. Steer the top 10 of each on 20 held-out prompts, keywords banned; a blind judge from the other model, human-checked, scores meme and coherence. Paired permutation test across memes.
rivals: Random same-layer units; a difference-of-means direction from the same pairs; a prompt asking for the meme (ceiling); a keyword list on the detection half. Most dangerous: the direction. If it both reads and writes while single units do one or neither, the meme is a direction, not a neuron.
premise: P1. If detectors do not write, 'which neurons fire' is a sensor reading and editing needs separately found units. If they do, one unit serves both, the strongest form of P1.
cost: S to M. Three to five days on the laptop; the writer screen is forward passes only, a few hours.
payoff: A rule for choosing edit handles, and a verdict on whether the study's detector units can be reused for engineering at all. It also records whether writers detect, and whether a detector fires when the model is simply asked to write its meme.
risk: Writers are picked by the kind of push they are then tested on, so part of their lead over detectors is built in; the informative numbers are the overlap and detectors against random units. In 4-bit models the dose window may be too narrow for either set.
review: Writers were picked by gradient attribution, which Liu 2026 reports mispredicts control; now a direct push screen on tuning prompts. Added the keyword ban, a human check and the study's own 18 units. Remaining weakness: writers' lead is partly built in by how they are chosen.
sources: Arad, Mueller, Belinkov 2025, arXiv:2505.20063; Kran Research 2026, Evil Qwen replication (blog.kran.ai/evil-qwen); HedwigAI 2026, Qwen personality neurons; Liu 2026, arXiv:2606.19831

title: Breeding captions on an archived fitness landscape
question: When a score-and-select loop may only move among captions that real people already rated, does scoring with model-internal units find funnier captions than scoring with embeddings or an LLM judge?
hypothesis: A tie. After 10 generations the unit-scored loop's final 20 captions sit within 3 percentile points of the embedding-scored loop's in real crowd rating, and both beat random selection by at least 5 points.
falsifier: The unit-scored loop ends more than 3 percentile points above or below the embedding-scored loop, with a 95% interval excluding zero across 100 held-out contests; a tie is claimed only if the whole interval sits within 3 points. Or no loop beats random selection by 5 points: caption text alone carries no breedable signal.
data: New Yorker caption contest rankings (Zhang et al. 2024; Hugging Face `yguooo/newyorker_caption_ranking`): 365 contests, over 2.2 million captions, over 250 million crowd ratings, plus a text description of each cartoon.
